title: What is agentic coding?
text:
Until recently, using an LLM meant typing into a chat box and copy-pasting the answer back into your editor. That works, but it puts you in the loop for every small action: copy this, paste here, run it, paste the error back, ask again. “Agentic coding” tools cut that loop. You give the model direct access to your project — it can read files, edit them, run code, see the output, and decide what to do next. You stay in the loop for direction and review, not for clerical handoffs.
That is the whole shift. Everything else on this site is a consequence of it.

title: What is agentic coding?
text:
A concrete contrast






Chat-style (what you might be doing now)

You: “Write me a Stata loop that runs a regression for each year and stores coefficients.”
LLM: (gives a snippet)
You: (paste into Stata, hit run, get an error about a missing variable)
You: “I got this error: variable wage_resid not found”
LLM: (apologizes, gives a new snippet)
You: (paste, run, repeat 3 more times)










Agentic (what Claude Code does)

You: “Write a loop that runs my main regression for each year and stores the coefficients. Look at analysis.do to see how I’ve set up the covariates.”
Claude Code: (reads analysis.do, writes the loop, runs it, sees the wage_resid not found error, reads 02-build-vars.do, notices that wage_resid is generated only when a flag is set, fixes the loop, runs it again, shows you the diff and the resulting coefficients)




The chat version takes ten minutes of attention. The agentic version takes ten minutes of clock time but maybe one minute of yours.

title: What is agentic coding?
section: What you give up, and what you keep
text:
What you give up, and what you keep
You give up the moment-by-moment control of every keystroke. You can’t inspect the model’s reasoning step by step in real time, and you have to trust that it’s editing the right files in the right way.
You keep — and must exercise — direction and review. You decide what to ask for. You read the diff before accepting it. You run the regression yourself before believing the number. The page on verifying output is the most important one on this site.

title: What is agentic coding?
section: Why this matters for an economist specifically
text:
Why this matters for an economist specifically
Three reasons it lands harder in our field than most:

Our work is heavy on small, tedious code. Renaming variables across a dozen .do files, regenerating tables in a different format, fixing a bibtex file with 200 entries — these are exactly the kinds of jobs where the agentic loop pays off.
Reproducibility matters. The model can read your whole replication package and tell you what’s missing or what won’t run on a fresh machine. A human RA would take a day; the model takes minutes.
You probably have several projects in different languages. The same tool works on Stata, R, Python, Matlab, Julia, LaTeX, and shell scripts — you don’t need to learn a different assistant for each.

title: Verifying output
text:
Warning



This is the page that matters most. Every other shortcut is fine if you do this one thing. Skip this and you will eventually publish something wrong with your name on it.

title: Verifying output
text:
The rule
Read the diff. Run the code. Open the file. Compare to your expectation.
Every time, even when you’re tired.

title: Verifying output
section: Outline — what “verify” means in concrete cases
text:
Outline — what “verify” means in concrete cases

Code edits

Read the diff before accepting. Quarto, Stata, R, Python, LaTeX — doesn’t matter. If you’re not reading diffs, you’re not in control.
For multi-file changes, read every file’s diff. The boring ones are where the bugs hide.



Numerical output

If Claude reports a coefficient, re-run the regression yourself in your usual environment before believing it. Cloud LLMs can confidently report numbers from a hallucinated run.
For estimation, save random seeds explicitly and confirm reproducibility on a re-run.



Citations and references

Any new \cite{...} Claude adds: confirm the entry exists in your .bib and that the cited paper actually says what you’re attributing to it. See Hallucinations.



Files that disappear

For deletions, refactors, or replication-package reorganization, work in a copy, not in your live project. Or use git: commit before, branch, and you can always undo.

title: Verifying output
section: Outline — habits that make verification cheap
text:
Outline — habits that make verification cheap

Use git. Even if you don’t push to GitHub, commit locally before any big change so git diff is meaningful. (Never used Git? See Git, for economists who’ve never used it — half an hour to learn, decades of payoff.)
Use plan mode for multi-file changes. Reading a plan first and then reviewing the diffs that match it is much easier than parsing surprise edits.
Run the build/test after every change. If your project has a make or a master do file, ask Claude to run it after each meaningful edit.

title: The terminal and bash, for GUI users
text:
Most economists I know have spent a career in graphical software: the Stata window with its menus, Matlab’s IDE, RStudio, Excel. None of those require you to think about the terminal. So when Claude Code starts typing things like Rscript analysis.R or git status in a black window, it can feel like a different planet.
It isn’t. The terminal is just the original way to talk to a computer: type a command, hit Return, see the output. There are no menus and no icons — just text in, text out. This page covers the minimum terminal vocabulary you need to (a) follow what Claude Code is doing on your behalf, and (b) type the few commands you’ll actually need yourself.
crumbs: The terminal and bash, for GUI users

title: The terminal and bash, for GUI users
text:
What “the terminal” actually is
A terminal is just a window where you type a command and your computer runs it. That’s the whole concept.

The window is called a terminal emulator (on a Mac, it’s the app called Terminal; iTerm and Warp are popular alternatives).
Inside that window, a small program called a shell is reading what you type and running it. On modern Macs the default shell is zsh. On Linux and on most Windows-WSL setups it’s bash. The two are nearly identical for our purposes; people use the names interchangeably.
Each line you type is a command — usually a program name, sometimes followed by arguments (what to run it on) and flags (options starting with - or --).

So when you see Claude Code run:
Rscript --vanilla analysis.R
That’s three pieces: the program (Rscript), a flag (--vanilla, meaning “don’t load my personal R settings”), and the file to run (analysis.R).

The fastest way:

Press Cmd + Space to open Spotlight.
Type Terminal and hit Return.
A small window with a blinking cursor appears.

You’ll see something like:

That’s the prompt, telling you it’s ready for a command. Type a command, hit Return.

Example

section: What “bash” really is, in one paragraph
text:
What “bash” really is, in one paragraph
A “bash script” (or “shell script”) is just a plain-text file with a list of these commands in it. When you “run” the script, the shell goes through the file line by line and runs each command in order. That’s all. A master.do file is a Stata script. A .bash or .sh file is a shell script. Same idea, different language.
Claude Code can read your shell scripts, write new ones, and run them. It can also string together one-off commands without writing a script. You don’t need to learn shell scripting to use Claude Code — but knowing it exists helps you read what Claude is doing.

What Claude Code actually runs in your terminal
When you watch Claude Code work, you’ll see it call out tools. The most common one is Bash, which means “run this in the terminal”. For econ-research projects, the commands you’ll see most are:
# Inspecting a project
ls
pwd
cat README.md
git status                  # what files have changed since last save
git diff paper.tex          # what specifically changed in paper.tex

# Running your code
Rscript scripts/01-clean.R              # run an R script
stata-mp -b master.do                   # run a Stata .do file in batch mode
python -m statsmodels analysis.py       # run a Python script
matlab -batch "run('main.m')"           # run a Matlab file

You don’t need to memorize any of these. section: A quick note on sed — text editing from the command line
text:
A quick note on sed — text editing from the command line
sed (“stream editor”) is a small program that edits text without opening a file in an editor. You will see it in inherited scripts; you will occasionally see Claude Code reach for it when doing the same mechanical change across many files at once.
It looks intimidating because the syntax is dense, but 95% of what anyone uses sed for is one pattern: find and replace.

The one pattern you’ll see
sed 's/OLD/NEW/g' file.txt
In English: “in file.txt, substitute NEW for every occurrence of OLD, and print the result.” The s means substitute; the g means globally (every match on each line, not just the first).
By default, sed prints the modified text to the terminal — your file on disk is not changed. To actually save the change back, add -i (“in-place”):
sed -i 's/OLD/NEW/g' file.txt          # Linux / WSL
sed -i '' 's/OLD/NEW/g' file.txt       # macOS (note the empty '')






Warning



Mac vs. Linux foot-gun. macOS uses BSD sed; Linux uses GNU sed. The -i flag works differently on each. On macOS you must follow -i with an empty string '' (the “backup suffix”). On Linux you don’t. This bites everyone the first time. If you’re following a script written on a Linux machine and sed -i complains “extra characters at the end of l command”, that’s the bug.




Examples relevant to econ work
Rename a variable across every .do file in a folder:
sed -i '' 's/wage_resid/wage_residual/g' *.do      # macOS
Strip carriage returns from a file your coauthor sent from Windows (causes mysterious LaTeX errors):
sed -i '' 's/\r$//' paper.tex
Replace a hardcoded path in a script:
sed -i '' 's|/Users/coauthor/Dropbox|/Users/me/Dropbox|g' master.do
Note the | separator instead of / in the last example — sed accepts any character as the separator, and | is much more readable when the pattern itself contains slashes (like a file path).


When Claude uses sed and when it doesn’t
For editing your project files, Claude Code prefers its own Edit tool — it shows you a clean diff per change and is harder to misuse. You’ll mostly see Claude reach for sed when:

The same change applies to many files at once (e.g., rename a variable in 30 .do files).
The edit is in a file Claude shouldn’t keep “in memory” (a multi-GB log file, for example).
A user has explicitly asked it to use the command line.

If you see Claude run sed -i against a file you care about, that change is not going through the diff-review path you’re used to. Verify the result with git diff afterwards, or commit before letting Claude run it so git checkout . is your undo button.

title: The terminal and bash, for GUI users
text:
Searching with grep
grep is the search tool. Give it a pattern and one or more files; it prints the matching lines. Read-only — it never changes anything — so it’s safe to type freely.
The basic pattern:
grep "wage_resid" analysis.do
In English: “show me every line in analysis.do that contains wage_resid.”
The flags you’ll actually use:







Flag
What it does




-r
Recursive — search inside every file in a folder and its subfolders


-n
Show line numbers next to each match


-i
Case-insensitive


-l
List only the filenames that match (not the matching lines)


-v
Invert — show lines that don’t match


--include="*.do"
Only look in files matching this pattern



In practice, grep -rn is the workhorse — recursive search with line numbers. Once you have it in your fingers, it replaces a lot of “where did I define this variable” cmd-F’ing across files.

Examples relevant to econ work
Find every place a variable is used across a project:
grep -rn "wage_resid" .
Find which .do files reference a particular dataset:
grep -rln "clean_data_v2.dta" --include="*.do" .
Find every TODO or FIXME comment a coauthor left in the code:
grep -rn -E "TODO|FIXME|XXX" .
Check whether a particular paper is cited in your manuscript:
grep -rn "smith2024" paper.tex appendix.tex
List every .bib entry by author surname (rough but fast):
grep "^@" references.bib | head      # entry types
grep "author = " references.bib | head


When Claude uses grep and when it doesn’t
Claude Code has a dedicated Grep tool that’s faster and friendlier than shelling out to grep (it uses ripgrep under the hood). You’ll usually see Claude use that instead. You’ll see actual grep in scripts written by humans, in old replication packages, and occasionally when Claude is piping output through several commands at once.
Either way, the mental model is the same: grep finds; it doesn’t change anything. If you typed it and you don’t like the result, type something else. There’s no recovery to do.

title: The terminal and bash, for GUI users
text:
Column work with awk
awk is the tool for column-oriented text — CSV files, log files, TSVs, anything where you care about “the third whitespace-separated field on each line.” It’s a tiny programming language in disguise. You will use 5% of it; that 5% is genuinely useful.
By default, awk splits each line on whitespace and exposes the columns as $1, $2, $3, … with $0 being the whole line.
The basic pattern:
awk '{print $3}' file.txt          # print the 3rd column of every line
For CSVs (or any non-whitespace separator) use -F:
awk -F',' '{print $1, $4}' data.csv      # 1st and 4th comma-separated columns

The four patterns that cover most use
# 1. Print specific columns
awk '{print $1, $5}' file.txt

# 2. Filter rows by a column condition
awk '$3 > 100' data.csv               # rows where column 3 > 100

# 3. Sum a column
awk '{sum += $2} END {print sum}' data.csv

# 4. Count rows matching a condition
awk '$3 == "treatment"' data.csv | wc -l
The END {...} block runs once after all lines are read — that’s how you accumulate totals or counts. There’s also a BEGIN {...} block that runs before any input.


Examples relevant to econ work
Quickly peek at one column of a 10 GB CSV without loading it into R or Stata:
awk -F',' '{print $7}' huge_admin_data.csv | head
Count distinct values in a column (rough but fast):
awk -F',' '{print $3}' data.csv | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
Sanity-check a sum from a Stata table against the underlying data:
awk -F',' 'NR>1 {sum += $4} END {print "Mean wage:", sum/(NR-1)}' wages.csv
(The NR>1 skips the header row; NR is awk’s built-in row counter.)
Extract just the variable names from a Stata describe log:
awk '/^[a-z]/ {print $1}' describe.log


Honest framing
awk is rarely the right tool when you have R, Python, or Stata already loaded. Its real niche is the in-between moment: you want a quick number from a file, and starting a full session in your stats language is overkill. For that — and for one-liners that Claude Code writes for you in a script — it’s hard to beat.
Like grep, plain awk is read-only; it prints to the terminal. It only modifies a file if you explicitly redirect output (> newfile.txt) or chain it through sed -i.

title: The terminal and bash, for GUI users
section: Other text tools you’ll see in passing
text:
Other text tools you’ll see in passing
You don’t need to learn these, but recognize them when they go by:

tr 'A' 'B' — character-by-character translation. Useful for uppercasing, stripping punctuation, normalizing line endings.
cut -f3 -d',' — extract a column from a delimited file. Like a one-trick awk for the “I just want column 3” case.
sort and uniq — sort lines, then collapse duplicates. The sort | uniq -c | sort -rn pattern (used in the awk example above) is the canonical “frequency table from a column” idiom.
xargs — take a list of things from stdin and run a command on each. Common with find ... | xargs grep ....

For all of these, the rule is the same: read what they do; let Claude write them; verify the output.

title: The terminal and bash, for GUI users
section: Safety: commands to never type without thinking
text:
Safety: commands to never type without thinking
Most terminal commands are harmless. A few are not. Treat the following the way you’d treat a power tool — fine when you mean to use it, dangerous when you don’t:






Warning



rm -rf <folder> — recursively, forcefully deletes a folder and everything inside it. No trash, no undo. Especially dangerous near ~, /, or * wildcards. Claude Code will prompt before doing this; don’t blanket-allow it.
sudo <anything> — runs the command as the system administrator. Almost never necessary for econ-research workflows. If something is asking you to sudo, slow down and figure out why. (The most common honest reason is sudo apt install on Linux to install software.)
chmod 777 <file> — makes a file readable, writable, and executable by everyone. The internet is full of “fix it with chmod 777” advice that “fixes” the problem by making your machine less safe. Don’t.
curl ... | bash or wget ... | sh — downloads code from the internet and immediately runs it without you reading it. Even from “trusted” sources, this is risky. Download first, read, then run.
git push --force to a shared branch — overwrites your coauthors’ work with no warning. If you’re sharing a repo, never force-push without talking to your coauthors first.
sed -i ... (or any in-place edit) without a git commit first — silently rewrites the file with no diff and no undo. The fix is a one-second habit: git add -A && git commit -m "before sed" before any sed -i you didn’t write yourself. See the sed section above.


The pattern: be suspicious whenever a command is destructive, privileged, or fetched from the internet and run sight-unseen. For everything else, the worst case is usually “type it again”.

title: The terminal and bash, for GUI users
section: When to let Claude drive vs. type yourself
text:
When to let Claude drive vs. type yourself
A pragmatic rule of thumb:

Reading commands (ls, pwd, cat, git status, git diff) — always fine for Claude to run automatically. They can’t break anything.
Building / running code (Rscript, stata-mp -b, latexmk) — fine for Claude to run, but watch for the failure mode where the script has side effects (writes files, sends an email, etc.). The first time you run a script under Claude, watch what it does.
Edits to your project files — Claude does these via its Edit and Write tools, which show you a diff. Read the diff. Always.
Destructive shell commands (rm, mv over an existing file, git checkout that discards work) — Claude prompts. Don’t blanket-allow.
git push, git push --force, deploying anything — type yourself, always. These are visible to other people. Make the decision consciously.

title: The terminal and bash, for GUI users
text:
A five-minute exercise
Open Terminal. Type each of these in order; press Return after each:
pwd
cd ~/Desktop
ls
mkdir terminal-test
cd terminal-test
echo "I survived the terminal" > note.txt
cat note.txt
cd ..
ls
You just: checked where you were, moved to your Desktop, listed the contents, made a folder, moved into it, created a text file in it, read the file, went back up one level, and listed the contents again. That is the entire terminal vocabulary you need to start using Claude Code.
When you’re done, you can clean up:
rm terminal-test/note.txt
rmdir terminal-test
(Note: rmdir only removes empty folders, so it’s safer than rm -rf.)

text: This page walks you through getting Claude Code on your machine and running it for the first time. It assumes you have never used the terminal in anger before. If you’re a terminal regular, skim past the basics.

title: Install Claude Code
text:
What you need

A Mac, a Windows machine with WSL, or a Linux box. (Most economists are on a Mac; the rest of this page assumes that. The differences for Windows/Linux are tiny and noted where they matter.)
An Anthropic account at claude.ai. A free account works to start; you’ll be prompted to set up billing the first time you use Claude Code.
About 20 minutes.

title: Install Claude Code
text:
Step 1 — Open a terminal
On a Mac:

Press Cmd + Space to open Spotlight.
Type Terminal and hit Return.
A small window with a blinking prompt appears. That’s your terminal.







Tip



The terminal is just another app. It can’t do anything you didn’t ask it to. The only commands you’ll need are the ones on this page; you don’t need to learn the rest.

title: Install Claude Code
section: Step 2 — Install Node.js (if you don’t have it)
text:
Step 2 — Install Node.js (if you don’t have it)
Claude Code is distributed as a Node.js package. Check whether you already have Node:
node --version
If that prints something like v20.11.0, you’re set — skip to Step 3.
If it says “command not found”, install Node from nodejs.org. Pick the LTS download, run the installer, accept the defaults. When it’s done, close and reopen the terminal, then re-run node --version to confirm.






Note



Mac users with Homebrew can install with brew install node instead. Windows users install Node inside WSL, not on Windows directly.

title: Install Claude Code
text:
Step 3 — Install Claude Code
In the terminal, run:
npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code
This downloads Claude Code and makes the claude command available system-wide. It takes a minute or two. When it’s done, verify:
claude --version






Warning



If you see a permission error mentioning EACCES or permission denied, don’t prefix the command with sudo. Instead, follow the npm fix-permissions instructions. This is a one-time fix and protects you from a class of problems later.

title: Install Claude Code
section: Step 4 — Point Claude Code at one of your projects
text:
Step 4 — Point Claude Code at one of your projects
Pick a project folder you’d like Claude Code to work in. Do not start with your most sensitive project. Pick a paper draft, a teaching repo, or a side project. In the terminal, change into that folder:
cd ~/Desktop/some-paper-draft
Then run:
claude
The first time you run it, you’ll be prompted to log in (a browser tab will open) and to choose a few preferences. Accept the defaults.
You’re now at the Claude Code prompt. It looks like a chat input but everything you type is being read by an agent that can see — and edit — the files in this folder.

title: Install Claude Code
section: Step 5 — Try it on something small
text:
Step 5 — Try it on something small
Three good first prompts, in increasing order of “letting it do things”:






Prompt 1 — read-only

“What is in this folder? Give me a one-paragraph summary of what this project does.”

Claude will list files, peek at a few, and summarize. You’ll see it call out tools like Read and Bash. Nothing is modified.









Prompt 2 — small edit, with review

“Add a comment at the top of every .do file naming the script and what it does. Show me each diff before applying.”

Claude proposes a change per file; you approve or reject each one.









Prompt 3 — real work

“Read paper.tex and tell me which references in the bibliography are never cited. Then remove the unused ones.”

This reads files, runs analysis, and edits. You approve the deletion.

title: Install Claude Code
text:
Step 6 — Quit and come back
To leave a Claude Code session, type /exit or press Ctrl-C twice.
To come back later, just cd into the same folder and run claude again. Claude Code keeps a memory of your project (in a file called CLAUDE.md, covered later) so the next session doesn’t start from zero.

Outline

1. Plan mode

title: What you must still do yourself
text:
The list

Specification
What’s the right model? What controls? What functional form? What sample restriction? Claude can implement any of these; it cannot tell you which is correct for your question.


Identification
Why does this design recover a causal effect? What threats remain? What robustness checks address them? The model can list textbook threats; it cannot judge whether your setting has them.


Interpretation
What does the coefficient mean? Is it economically large? Is it consistent with prior estimates? What’s the policy or theoretical takeaway? Claude can produce confident-sounding interpretations that are wrong about your context.


Contribution
What’s new here? Why should anyone care? Where does this sit in the literature? Claude has read a lot but has no taste — it cannot tell you whether your contribution is interesting.


Authorship
Anything you submit goes out under your name. Claude is not a co-author; it’s a tool. Don’t list it; don’t pretend it didn’t help; do disclose LLM use as your journal requires.


The hard problem
The model is good enough that you’ll be tempted to outsource judgment disguised as code: “write the empirical strategy section”, “decide which controls to include”, “write the limitations section”. Notice when you’re about to do this. The cost of bad judgment doesn’t go down because the typing got faster.

title: LLMs for Economists
text:
This is a colleagues-only field guide to a particular way of using LLMs: giving an AI agent direct access to your project files so it can write code, edit your LaTeX, audit a replication package, and run things on your behalf — under your supervision.
It is not about chatting with ChatGPT in a browser. That is useful too, but it isn’t what’s changed in the last year.

title: LLMs for Economists
text:
Who this is for
You are an economist who:

Spends real hours writing Stata/R/Python/Matlab/Julia code, formatting LaTeX papers, building tables, or wrangling a replication package.
Has heard “AI agents” get hyped and would like a non-marketing explanation of what’s actually useful and what is not.
Wants the shortest possible path from “I’ve heard of Claude Code” to “Claude Code is editing my paper while I review the diff.”

You don’t need to know git, the terminal, or any web technology beyond the basics. We’ll cover the parts that matter.

Start here →

section: A note on what’s “fleshed out” right now
text:
A note on what’s “fleshed out” right now
This site is a living draft. The two long-form examples (LaTeX paper editing and replication-package audit) and the install guide are the most complete. Other pages are short outlines that I’ll fill in as colleagues use them and tell me what’s missing. If you find a section that would help you and isn’t there yet, tell me — that’s the fastest way to make this useful.

title: Principles
text:
So I thought I will put my thoughts in here after our department meeting with the help of Claude Code. Most of this is based on my experience of using chatbot AI and agentic AI. So most of my thoughts are based on my usage of LLM products from Anthropic (Claude, Claude Code), OpenAI (Chat GPT, Codex) and a little of Github (Github copilot). I use Claude most of the times. The efficiency gains that can be had depends heavily on how our workflow is aligned with how large language models (LLMs) work.
The difference between chatbot AI tools like Claude (and Chat GPT) and agentic AI like Claude code (and Codex) is that in the former you are in a chat session and in the latter the AI does stuff on your behalf and uses your computer to implement stuff using Bash scripts, after you give it directory level permissions to run things. The major efficiency gains come from using agentic AI over chatbot AI. In the latter there is a wide variety of how much you let your LLM do your work. I used to think that this depends on how risk averse you are. But in my experience, I think it more depends on how detailed your prompting is such that the LLM understands the context, how robust your system such that it has fail-safes, and how do you design your workflow so that the agent can verify its own work and can hence iterate on its mistakes minimizing your intervention.
The rest of this page expands on those three things, because they are what I would have wanted someone to tell me a year ago.

title: Principles
text:
1. Detailed prompting and context
The single biggest predictor of whether Claude Code does something useful on the first try is whether I gave it enough context to understand what I actually want. “Detailed prompting” is not a euphemism for writing long prompts. It means giving the model the information a smart RA would need to do the job — no more, no less.
In practice, this is three things:

Name the files. “Read paper.tex and tell me…” beats “look at my paper” every time. The model can find files; it cannot read your mind about which one you mean.
State the constraint, not just the goal. “Reformat all my tables using booktabs” is the goal. “Reformat all my tables using booktabs; do not change any numbers, captions, or column headers” is the constraint that prevents Claude from “tidying up” content you didn’t ask it to tidy.
Provide stable context once, not every session. A CLAUDE.md file at the root of your project — saying which Stata version you use, which scripts produce which outputs, what’s off-limits — is read at the start of every session. Writing it once saves you re-explaining. See Memory, CLAUDE.md, skills.

The mental model that helped me: a chatbot prompt is a Google query, but an agentic prompt is a memo to a new RA on day one. Different audience, different register.
What this looks like in our examples:

The first paragraph of every prompt in the LaTeX paper walkthrough is an orientation pass — having Claude read the project before doing anything.
The replication-package audit starts by asking Claude to describe the dependency map before changing anything. The audit is the context for the action.

title: Principles
text:
2. A robust system with fail-safes
This was the principle that took me longest to internalize because it requires admitting up front that the model will sometimes do the wrong thing — and designing your environment so a wrong action is recoverable rather than catastrophic.
The fail-safes I rely on are not exotic:

Git, even just locally. I commit before any non-trivial change. If Claude makes an edit I don’t like, git checkout . undoes everything in the working directory. You don’t need to push to GitHub for this to save you. (If you’ve never used Git, the Git for the never-used-it page is the shortest path from zero to using it as a daily safety net.)
Plan mode. For any change touching multiple files, I hit Shift+Tab until the prompt says “plan mode”. Claude reads, thinks, and writes a plan for my approval. I read the plan; if it misunderstands, I correct before any file is touched. See Plan mode, todos, slash commands.
Don’t blanket-allow destructive operations. Claude Code prompts before things like deleting files, force-pushing to git, or running rm -rf. Don’t override those prompts. The two-second pause is the difference between a recoverable mistake and a Saturday spent reconstructing your project from memory.
A working “master script” in every project. A single master.do, master.R, or make all that rebuilds your results from scratch. After any meaningful change, ask Claude to re-run it and confirm outputs match. This is your reproducibility check and your fail-safe.
Read-only patterns for restricted data. When I work on projects with IRB-protected or restricted-access data, Claude only ever sees the code, never the data. The data lives in a folder Claude is not pointed at. See Confidential data.

A useful test: before starting a task, ask yourself “if Claude does the worst plausible thing here, what is my recovery?” If the answer is “git checkout”, you’re fine. If the answer is “rebuild from backups” or “email my coauthor”, slow down and add a fail-safe first.

title: Principles
section: 3. A workflow the agent can verify on its own
text:
3. A workflow the agent can verify on its own
This is the principle with the highest payoff and the one most colleagues miss. The point is not to write better prompts. It is to structure the task so the agent can check its own work — and then iterate without needing you in the loop for every step.
A few examples of what this looks like in econ work:

Replication. “Re-run master.do and tell me whether each table in output/tables/ matches the version checked into git.” The agent runs the script, diffs the outputs, and either reports “all match” or “Table 3 changed — here’s the diff”. One human-readable status; no per-step babysitting.
Cleaning. Add assertions to your cleaning scripts: assert wage > 0 if inrange(year, 2000, 2020). When Claude edits the cleaning code and an assertion fails, the script halts and the agent sees exactly what broke. It can iterate to fix the bug without you.
LaTeX. After every edit to a .tex file, Claude can compile and read the log. Unresolved references, overfull boxes, missing citations — all surface immediately, and the agent can either fix them or escalate to you.
Numerical work. A test that checks the sign and rough magnitude of the main coefficient (not its exact value) is enough for Claude to notice when a refactor silently breaks the analysis.
Code review. For non-trivial edits I ask Claude to run /review on its own diff before showing it to me. It catches its own clumsy edits about half the time.

When this principle is in place, my supervision shifts from “every keystroke” to “every milestone”. I check in when the agent reports something done, not while it works.

title: Principles
text:
Putting it together
These three principles compound. Detailed prompting alone is wasted if the agent can’t recover from a wrong turn. Fail-safes alone keep you safe but not productive. Self-verification alone is impossible without context to verify against.
The way I’d phrase it now, after a year of this:

The efficiency you get from agentic AI is roughly (quality of context) × (recoverability of the system) × (degree to which the agent can check its own work). If any one of those is near zero, your effective productivity gain is near zero too — even if the model is brilliant.

Most of my own learning has been about raising the third factor. The model is plenty capable; the bottleneck has been giving it the scaffolding to use that capability without me hovering over it.

title: Principles
text:
Where to go from here

The most concrete application of all three principles at once is reorganizing a messy project — context (a fresh inventory), recoverability (a copy plus git), and self-verification (a master script the agent can re-run) are all built into the walkthrough.
See these principles applied end-to-end in the replication-package audit and the LaTeX paper walkthrough.
For the operational habits — what to type, what to leave alone, when to hit plan mode — see How to ask and Verifying output.
For what these principles don’t protect you from — research judgment, identification, interpretation — see What you must still do.

title: Hallucinations
text:
Warning



Coming soon. A field guide to the specific kinds of hallucinations that hurt empirical economists, and the verification habits that catch each one.

title: Hallucinations
text:
Outline — what gets hallucinated

1. Citations and references

Bibliography entries that don’t exist.
Cited claims that the paper doesn’t actually make.
Slightly wrong years, page numbers, or author orders.

Catch: before any new \cite{...} lands in your paper, open the source paper and confirm.


2. Regression results

Coefficients reported without the regression having actually been run.
“I ran your model and got…” when no Bash tool call was made.

Catch: re-run the regression yourself, or insist Claude show you the log/output from a real run.


3. Function and option names

A Stata command that doesn’t exist, or has a different syntax than Claude reports.
An R function from the wrong package, or with arguments that don’t exist.
A LaTeX package that doesn’t behave the way Claude described.

Catch: for unfamiliar commands, check the documentation. For Stata: help <command>. For R: ?fn or the package’s website.


4. File contents

A claim about what’s in a file that Claude didn’t actually read.

Catch: Claude shows you tool calls. If it claims to have looked at paper.tex but you don’t see a Read tool call for it, push back: “Did you actually read it? Show me.”


5. Replication-package completeness

“I ran the master script and everything worked” when it didn’t.
“All your tables are reproduced” without checking.

Catch: diff the produced output against what’s in your paper.

title: Hallucinations
text:
The general rule
Claude is a confident colleague who occasionally lies with no self-awareness. Treat its outputs the way you’d treat a draft from a new RA on day one: gratefully, and with full verification.

title: Confidential and restricted-access data
text:
Warning



Read this page before pointing Claude Code at any project containing IRB-protected, restricted-access, or otherwise confidential data. When in doubt, default to “no” and ask your IRB.

title: Confidential and restricted-access data
text:
Outline — what to never send

IRB-protected human-subjects data (interviews, identifiable surveys, health data) unless your IRB protocol explicitly permits cloud LLM processing — most don’t.
FERPA-covered student records.
Restricted-access administrative data (Census, IRS, state longitudinal data systems, etc.) — almost universally prohibited from any cloud transmission. RDC/FSRDC environments forbid it outright.
Confidential firm or proprietary data under NDA.
Refereed manuscripts without checking journal policy.

title: Confidential and restricted-access data
text:
Outline — what is generally safe

Public datasets (IPUMS, Compustat extracts you’d freely share, BLS microdata releases, etc.).
Your own simulated data.
Code that doesn’t reveal the underlying observations.
Paper drafts on your own work (with co-author awareness).

title: Confidential and restricted-access data
text:
Outline — pragmatic workarounds
When you have a restricted dataset and want help with the code:

Synthesize a fake version. Have Claude generate fake data with the same schema and let it work on that.
Point it at code only, never data. Most “clean this .do file” work doesn’t need the actual data; it needs the script.
Run sensitive jobs on the secure environment with no cloud LLM involved, then bring back outputs you’re allowed to share.
Use Claude Code only for non-restricted side projects until you’ve talked to your IRB about an explicit policy.

title: Confidential and restricted-access data
text:
Outline — institutional questions to resolve

Does your university have a policy on LLM use with research data?
Does your IRB have boilerplate language for cloud LLM processing?
Do data agreements (DUAs) you’ve signed permit transmission to third-party services?

title: Using Claude Code inside VS Code
text: If you’ve spent your career in graphical environments — RStudio, Stata’s window, Matlab’s IDE — running Claude Code in a bare terminal can feel like working with one hand tied behind your back. Visual Studio Code (“VS Code”) is the gentlest landing pad. It is free, it is graphical, it has a built-in terminal, it shows you proposed code edits in a normal side-by-side diff view, and it knows about Git. For most colleagues I recommend starting here — and dropping back to the bare terminal only if and when it stops getting in the way.

title: Using Claude Code inside VS Code
section: Why this is the easier starting point
text:
Why this is the easier starting point







In a bare terminal
In VS Code




Code edits show up as a wall of text diffs
Edits appear in a familiar side-by-side diff pane


File paths in Claude’s output are just strings
File paths are clickable; Cmd-click jumps you to line and column

The Source Control pane shows changes file-by-file in real time



None of these are revolutionary. Together they remove enough small friction that “I’ll try Claude Code today” stops feeling like a project of its own.

text:
Step 1 — Install VS Code
Download from code.visualstudio.com. The installer is signed and behaves like any other Mac app — drag to Applications, open, accept the security prompt the first time.
If your colleague already has VS Code, this step is a no-op.

title: Using Claude Code inside VS Code
section: Step 2 — Install the Claude Code extension
text:
Step 2 — Install the Claude Code extension
VS Code has an extension marketplace. The official Claude Code extension by Anthropic gives you in-editor integration with the CLI you installed earlier. It is optional — you can use Claude Code in VS Code’s integrated terminal without it — but it is a small install that pays for itself the first time you accept a diff inside the editor instead of squinting at one in the terminal.
To install:

Click the Extensions icon in the left sidebar (or press Cmd+Shift+X).
Search for Claude Code.
Install the one published by Anthropic.

What the extension adds (paraphrased — see the extension’s own page for the canonical list):

Native diff view. When Claude proposes an edit, the change opens in VS Code’s diff editor instead of being printed to the terminal. You approve or reject with a button.
Open-file and selection awareness. Claude can see which file you have focused and what you have selected, so prompts like “rewrite the highlighted paragraph” Just Work.

title: Git, for economists who’ve never used it
text:
If you’ve never used Git, this page is the most important one for you. Not because Git itself is interesting — it isn’t — but because Git is the safety net that makes letting Claude Code edit your project tolerable. Without Git, “Claude proposed a 200-line change across six files” is terrifying. With Git, it’s a question of “do I git checkout . or do I keep this?” — a yes/no decision that takes one keystroke to undo.
This page assumes you have never used Git in anger. If you have a GitHub account but only clone repositories occasionally, that counts as never. Read on.
crumbs: Git, for economists who've never used it

title: Git, for economists who’ve never used it
section: The mental model in two paragraphs
text:
The mental model in two paragraphs
Git is a time machine for a project folder. You decide when to take a snapshot — that’s a “commit.” Every commit is permanent, locally, forever. You can always come back to any past state. You don’t need to push to GitHub for any of this to work; “local Git” is enough to make the snapshots and the undo path.
Each commit has a short message (“fix Table 3 standard errors”), a date, an author, and a unique ID (a “hash” — a 7-character random string like 8dad523). Commits form a chain: each one is a delta from the previous one. When you want to know what changed when, or undo a change from yesterday, or remember what your paper looked like three weeks ago — git has the answer.
That’s it. Everything else is plumbing.
crumbs: Git, for economists who've never used it

title: Git, for economists who’ve never used it
section: Why this matters for using Claude Code
text:
Why this matters for using Claude Code
Three reasons Git is non-negotiable once you start using an agent on your projects:

Undoing. When Claude makes an edit you don’t like — and it will sometimes — git checkout -- file.tex puts the file back exactly as it was at the last commit. No memory required.
Reading the diff. Before accepting any non-trivial Claude edit, you want to see exactly what changed. git diff shows you.
Recovering from a bad day. When you discover a week later that a refactor broke a result, git log and git checkout <past-hash> take you back to a working state.

Without Git, your fail-safe is “I have a backup somewhere?” — which is not a fail-safe. With Git, your fail-safe is one command. That’s the robust system the principles page talks about.
crumbs: Git, for economists who've never used it

title: Git, for economists who’ve never used it
text:
Step 1 — Confirm Git is installed
On a Mac, Git ships pre-installed. In a terminal:
git --version
You should see something like git version 2.54.0. If not, the quickest fix is brew install git (if you have Homebrew) or downloading the installer from git-scm.com.
On Windows: install Git for Windows — it also gives you a usable bash terminal.
crumbs: Git, for economists who've never used it

title: Git, for economists who’ve never used it
section: Step 2 — Tell Git who you are (one-time setup)
text:
Step 2 — Tell Git who you are (one-time setup)
Git records who made each commit. Configure your name and email once, globally:
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@university.edu"
This is metadata, not authentication. It just labels your commits.
While you’re here, set the default branch name to main (the modern convention) and the default editor to something you can use:
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
git config --global core.editor "code --wait"   # if you use VS Code
# or "nano" if you'd rather not use VS Code as your git editor
You only do this once per machine.
crumbs: Git, for economists who've never used it

title: Git, for economists who’ve never used it
section: Step 3 — Initialize a Git repo in a project
text:
Step 3 — Initialize a Git repo in a project
cd into one of your project folders (one you’ve already reorganized — or any project you’d like a safety net under) and:
cd ~/Desktop/wage-paper
git init
That’s it. There’s now a hidden .git/ folder in your project that holds the entire history. You won’t ever look inside it.
Take the first snapshot, capturing the current state of everything:
git add -A
git commit -m "Initial commit"
Congratulations — you have a Git repository. There is now exactly one commit. Every change you make from this point on can be reviewed, diffed, and undone.






Tip



Run git init for every project, including teaching repos and side projects. It costs nothing and gives you the safety net everywhere. There is no downside to having a local-only Git history.
crumbs: Git, for economists who've never used it

title: Git, for economists who’ve never used it
text:
Step 4 — The daily loop
The cycle you’ll repeat constantly:
# 1. Work on your project (edit paper.tex, run analysis.do, whatever)

# 2. See what's changed since the last commit
git status

# 3. See the actual changes line-by-line
git diff

# 4. Decide what to commit. Either everything:
git add -A

# Or specific files:
git add paper.tex code/03-analysis.do

# 5. Take the snapshot
git commit -m "Update Table 3 with revised standard errors"
That’s the whole loop. Status → diff → add → commit. Do this several times a day, every day, on every project. Each commit is cheap and takes seconds.






Tip



Commit messages are notes to your future self. Treat them like the comment line at the top of a .do file. “Update results” is bad; “Fix Table 3 SE clustering at the firm level” is good. You’ll thank yourself when, six months later, you’re trying to figure out which commit broke the IV first stage.
crumbs: Git, for economists who've never used it

title: Git, for economists who’ve never used it
section: A first session, end to end
text:
A first session, end to end
Try this in any project:
cd ~/Desktop/some-project
git init
git add -A
git commit -m "Initial commit"

# Make a change — edit any file
echo "% added a comment" >> paper.tex

git status                    # tells you paper.tex is modified
git diff                      # shows the new line
git add paper.tex
git commit -m "Add a comment to paper.tex"

git log --oneline             # see your two commits
The whole thing takes two minutes. You now know enough Git to use it every day. Everything below is for the moments when something goes wrong — and those moments are when Git pays off most.
crumbs: Git, for economists who've never used it

title: Git, for economists who’ve never used it
text:
Reading the past
Once you have a few commits, the questions start: “what did this file look like last week?” “When did I change this?”
git log --oneline             # short list of every commit
git log paper.tex             # commits that touched paper.tex specifically
git show 8dad523              # the change made in commit 8dad523
git diff 8dad523              # diff against the state at commit 8dad523
git diff main~3 main          # diff between three commits ago and now
The ~3 notation means “three commits before”; main~3 is “three commits before the tip of main.” That’s the only weird syntax you’ll need for a while.
crumbs: Git, for economists who've never used it

title: Git, for economists who’ve never used it
text:
Undoing things — the safe operations
The five operations that cover almost every “oh no” moment:

Discard uncommitted changes to one file
You edited paper.tex, hated the result, want to go back to the last committed version:
git checkout -- paper.tex
Or, the modern equivalent (Git 2.23+):
git restore paper.tex
Either way, paper.tex is back to its last-committed state. The file you had on disk is gone.






Warning



This operation cannot be undone. The version on disk is overwritten. If the unsaved work mattered, you wanted to commit it (even on a “junk” branch) before discarding.




Discard ALL uncommitted changes
Same idea, broader. Wipes every uncommitted edit in the working tree:
git checkout .
Or:
git restore .
This is the canonical “Claude made a mess; start over from where I was” button.


Unstage a file (without losing changes)
You ran git add paper.tex but want to take it back without losing the edits:
git reset HEAD paper.tex
# or:
git restore --staged paper.tex
The file is no longer staged for the next commit, but your changes are still on disk.


See what a file looked like at a past commit
git show 8dad523:paper.tex > paper-from-may.tex
That writes the May version of paper.tex to a new file. You compare to the current one without disturbing anything.


Revert a single past commit
You committed 8dad523 last Tuesday and now want to undo just that change, without losing anything that came after:
git revert 8dad523
Git creates a new commit that’s the inverse of 8dad523. Safe; doesn’t rewrite history.
crumbs: Git, for economists who've never used it

title: Git, for economists who’ve never used it
text:
Undoing things — the destructive operations
These rewrite history. They’re sometimes the right tool, but they have sharp edges. Read carefully.






Warning



git reset --hard <hash> — moves the project back to the state at <hash> and discards every commit after it. Useful when you know the last few commits were a mistake; dangerous when you don’t.
git push --force — overwrites the remote branch with your local state, even if it diverges. Never do this on a shared branch without talking to coauthors first; it deletes their work from the remote.
git clean -fd — deletes every untracked file in the project. Useful when build artifacts are everywhere; dangerous because it can delete files Git has never seen and therefore cannot recover.








Tip



The safety net under the destructive operations: git reflog. Every state Git has ever been in is recorded in the “reflog” for 30 days, even after reset --hard. If you destroy work, the first thing to try is:
git reflog
That lists every state, with hashes. git checkout <hash> or git reset --hard <hash> brings you back. This has saved more careers than any other Git command.
crumbs: Git, for economists who've never used it

title: Git, for economists who’ve never used it
section: Branches — for trying things without breaking what works
text:
Branches — for trying things without breaking what works
Branches are alternate timelines. Useful for “let me try this big refactor without messing up the current paper draft.”
git checkout -b experiment        # create and switch to a new branch
# … work, commit, work, commit …
git checkout main                 # back to the main timeline
git merge experiment              # bring the experiment's commits into main
If you decide the experiment was a bad idea:
git checkout main
git branch -D experiment          # throw it away
For solo research projects, you’ll often skip branches entirely and just commit to main. That’s fine. Use branches when:

You want to try a structural change you might roll back.
You’re collaborating and want to share work-in-progress without disturbing the main line.
You’re preparing a replication package while still working on follow-ups.







Note



Merging is straightforward when nobody else has changed the same lines you did. When two people edit the same line, you get a “merge conflict” — Git asks you to choose between (or combine) the two versions. Don’t panic; this is a normal part of collaboration. Claude Code is good at walking you through resolving conflicts. See “When you’re stuck” below.
crumbs: Git, for economists who've never used it

title: Git, for economists who’ve never used it
text:
Going beyond your machine — GitHub
Everything above works with zero internet connection. Git is purely local. To back up your work, share with coauthors, or publish a replication package, you push to a “remote” — usually GitHub (github.com) but GitLab, Bitbucket, and self-hosted alternatives work the same way.

One-time setup per project
Create an empty repository on GitHub. It will give you a URL like https://github.com/yourname/wage-paper.git. In your local project:
git remote add origin https://github.com/yourname/wage-paper.git
git push -u origin main
The -u origin main part is shorthand for “remember that my local main corresponds to main on origin” — you only need it the first time.


The everyday loop, with a remote
When you’re working from one machine on a solo project, you don’t need to push every time. When you do push:
git push                    # send your commits to GitHub
git pull                    # fetch coauthors' commits and merge in
That’s the whole remote workflow. The vast majority of “Git frustration” in econ comes from forgetting to git pull before starting work — when you do, your commits and your coauthor’s commits diverge, and you have to do a merge.






Warning



Do not push your projects to a public GitHub repo without thinking about what’s in them. Anything in data/raw/ may include restricted-access or IRB-protected data. Anything in your code may include hardcoded paths revealing folder structures you’d rather not share. Default to private repos and only flip to public deliberately when you’re ready to publish a replication package. See Confidential data.
crumbs: Git, for economists who've never used it

title: Git, for economists who’ve never used it
text:
Coauthor workflow
Two coauthors editing the same project, each with their own laptop and a shared GitHub repo:

Always git pull before you start working. This brings their commits into your local copy.
Commit and push when you stop for the day. Tiny commits with real messages are infinitely better than one big “Update” commit at the end of the week.
If a git pull produces a merge conflict, Git will tell you exactly which files conflict. Open them; you’ll see markers like:
<<<<<<< HEAD
your version
=======
your coauthor's version
>>>>>>> main
Pick which one survives (or combine them), delete the markers, git add, git commit. Done.
Communicate before doing anything destructive on a shared branch. No git push --force, no git reset --hard of pushed commits, without a Slack/email/text first.

For most coauthorships, that’s it. You don’t need branches per collaborator unless the project gets complex.
crumbs: Git, for economists who've never used it

title: Git, for economists who’ve never used it
text:
What NOT to commit
A .gitignore file at the project root tells Git to skip these. The reorganize page’s Step 12 has a full template; the highlights:

Large data files. GitHub’s free tier limits files to 100 MB and repos to a soft 1 GB. For large datasets, use Git LFS or store the data outside the repo and document where it lives in the README.
Restricted-access or confidential data. Never commit it, full stop. See Confidential data.
Secrets / credentials. API keys, database passwords, anything ending in .pem or .key. If you ever commit one by accident, treat it as compromised and rotate it.
Derived outputs. data/derived/, output/tables/*.tex, paper/paper.pdf. These are reproducible from the source — no reason to track them.
Build artifacts. .aux, .log, .synctex.gz, *.smcl, __pycache__/, .Rhistory, etc.
crumbs: Git, for economists who've never used it

title: Git, for economists who’ve never used it
section: The friendly path: VS Code’s Source Control pane
text:
The friendly path: VS Code’s Source Control pane
If a colleague is going to use Git through a graphical interface, the best one is already inside VS Code. Open the Source Control pane (Ctrl+Shift+G or click the branching-tree icon in the left sidebar). You’ll see:

A list of every changed file, grouped by “Staged” and “Changes.”
Click any file to see the diff in the editor — same diff git diff prints, but pretty.
The + next to a file stages it. The - un-stages it.
The text box at the top is the commit message; the checkmark icon commits.
The … menu has push, pull, branch operations, etc.

For colleagues who’d rather not touch the CLI for git, this is the recommended path. The same operations happen under the hood; you just click instead of typing. See the VS Code page for the broader VS Code setup.






Note



Other graphical Git clients worth knowing about: GitHub Desktop (simplest; free; opinionated), GitKraken (powerful; free for academic use), Sourcetree (free; aging). All are fine. If you’re already in VS Code, you don’t need any of them.
crumbs: Git, for economists who've never used it

title: Git, for economists who’ve never used it
section: What Claude Code does with Git on your behalf
text:
What Claude Code does with Git on your behalf
Claude Code knows Git. When working in a project with git init-d already, it will:

Run git status and git diff on its own to see what’s changed.
Stage and commit files when you ask.
Create branches if you ask.
Read history with git log to understand the project’s evolution.

It will not:

Run git push without you asking explicitly.
Run any destructive operation (reset --hard, clean -fd, push --force) without prompting first.
Commit changes silently. By default, you see what it staged before the commit happens.

A useful default is to let Claude commit on your behalf for routine work (“commit the bibliography fix you just made”), but type git push yourself the first time it goes to a shared remote. Pushes are visible to other people; that one’s worth a conscious keypress.
crumbs: Git, for economists who've never used it

title: Git, for economists who’ve never used it
text:
When you’re stuck
The “I think I broke Git” recovery path:

Stop. Don’t run more commands. The single most common way to make a Git problem worse is to keep running git commands hoping one of them fixes it.
Run git status and read what it says. Git’s error messages, for all their reputation, are usually accurate and tell you the next command to run.
git reflog is your “undo undo.” Every state Git has been in is recorded for 30 days. If you destroyed something, it’s almost certainly in there. Find the hash you want; git checkout <hash> to inspect, git reset --hard <hash> to fully restore.
Ask Claude. Open Claude Code in the project, paste the output of git status and git reflog, and say what you were trying to do when things went wrong. Claude is genuinely good at Git diagnosis — it’s seen every variation of “I made a mess” before.
crumbs: Git, for economists who've never used it

title: Git, for economists who’ve never used it
text:
A word on git push --force
You will eventually hear someone tell you to git push --force to “fix” a problem. It will solve their immediate symptom and may delete your coauthors’ commits from the remote. Never run it on a shared branch without explicit talked-through agreement. If you must rewrite shared history, use git push --force-with-lease — it refuses to overwrite work you didn’t know about.
crumbs: Git, for economists who've never used it

title: Git, for economists who’ve never used it
section: What you skipped — and don’t need to come back to (yet)
text:
What you skipped — and don’t need to come back to (yet)
If you’re worried about gaps in your Git knowledge, here’s what you deliberately don’t need:

Rebase (git rebase) — rewrites history. Useful when you become fluent; harmful as a beginner. The Pro Git book has it when you’re ready.
Cherry-pick (git cherry-pick) — copying a single commit from one branch to another. You’ll learn it the day you actually need it.
Stash (git stash) — temporarily setting aside uncommitted changes. Convenient but skippable; you can always create a quick “WIP” commit instead.
Submodules — nested repos. Almost never the right tool for econ research. If a coauthor proposes them, push back.
Hooks — scripts that run on commits. You don’t need them.

These are real tools. They’re just not on your critical path.
