title: Reorganizing a messy project before letting Claude Code work on it
text:
If you’re like most economists, your active research folders look something like this:
There is no README. The “live” version of paper.tex is in your head, not on disk. The Stata cleaning scripts call into Julia for estimation and R for figures, but nothing documents the order. Three of the .do files run; one runs but produces the wrong table; the other two break. The Julia files in estimate_test.jl are an old structural model; the live one is in estimate.jl. Two of the .dta files are inputs to something; the rest are dead. Half the scripts have hardcoded paths to your coauthor’s Dropbox folder.
This is fine for a human who wrote it. It is bad for Claude Code, which will read everything, get confused about which version is canonical, and either ask you a lot of questions or — worse — confidently edit the wrong file.
This page walks you through a one-time reorganization that gets the project into shape for agentic work. It is itself a perfect first project for Claude Code, because the agent can do most of the work and the worst case is recoverable.
crumbs: Reorganizing a messy project before letting Claude Code work on it

title: Reorganizing a messy project before letting Claude Code work on it
section: What “ready for Claude Code” actually means
text:
What “ready for Claude Code” actually means
You are aiming for a project where:

A stranger (or a future-you, or an RA, or Claude Code) can open the folder and figure out what’s going on within five minutes.
There is a single master script that runs every step from raw data to final tables and the compiled paper.
Live code is clearly distinguished from old/exploratory code. The archive is preserved, not deleted.
Every dependency between files is explicit (no hidden assumptions about what was last run by hand in Stata’s window).
A CLAUDE.md file at the root tells Claude what’s specific to your project: language version, conventions, what’s off-limits, where the data is, what the master script is.
A README.md tells a human reader the same things.
.gitignore keeps derived files and OS junk out of git.
Git is initialized so any change is recoverable.

A reasonable target structure (adjust to taste):
project-name/
├── README.md
├── CLAUDE.md
├── .gitignore
├── make-all.sh           (top-level orchestrator; calls each language in order)
├── data/
│   ├── raw/              (read-only; never modified by code)
│   └── derived/          (built from raw/ by code/)
├── code/
│   ├── 01-clean.do          (Stata: prep raw data)
│   ├── 02-estimate.jl       (Julia: structural estimation)
│   ├── 03-counterfactuals.jl (Julia: simulate)
│   └── 04-figures.R         (R: ggplot tables and figures)
├── output/
│   ├── tables/
│   └── figures/
├── paper/
│   ├── paper.tex
│   ├── references.bib
│   └── (figures, tables, etc.)
├── docs/                 (data dictionaries, notes, source docs)
└── archive/              (everything you didn't delete but isn't live)
The single code/ folder mixes Stata, Julia, and R because that’s how the work flows — the numeric prefixes (01-, 02-, …) make the order obvious regardless of language. Some people prefer code/stata/, code/julia/, code/r/ subfolders instead; either works as long as the orchestrator at the top knows the order.
This is a default, not a religion. AEA, TIER, BITSS, and the Reardon protocol all propose variations — pick one and stick to it.
crumbs: Reorganizing a messy project before letting Claude Code work on it

title: Reorganizing a messy project before letting Claude Code work on it
text:
The 13-step walkthrough
Each step has the prompt you’d give Claude Code (in the integrated terminal of VS Code or in a bare terminal — your choice). Read every diff before approving.

Step 1 — Copy the project to a working directory
Do this in the terminal yourself, not through Claude. It is one command and it is the safety net for everything that follows.
cp -R ~/Dropbox/wage-paper ~/Desktop/wage-paper-cleanup
Or, on a Mac, use Finder: select the folder, Cmd-D to duplicate, move the duplicate somewhere outside Dropbox.






Warning



Move the copy outside any cloud-synced folder (Dropbox, OneDrive, iCloud Drive). Reorganization will rename and move many files; you don’t want every intermediate state syncing across your devices and your coauthors’ machines. Once you’re done and verified, you can move the finished version back.
If your project contains IRB-protected, restricted-access, or otherwise confidential data, stop and read Confidential data before doing anything else. At minimum, make sure the data subfolder is not pulled into the working copy unless you’ve confirmed it’s safe to send to a cloud LLM provider in subsequent steps.


Verify the copy:
du -sh ~/Dropbox/wage-paper ~/Desktop/wage-paper-cleanup
Sizes should match within a few KB. Now cd into the copy and from this point on, work only there.
cd ~/Desktop/wage-paper-cleanup


Step 2 — Initialize git in the copy
Even if you never push to GitHub, local git is the recoverable history that makes the rest of this walkthrough safe. From inside the copy:
git init -b main
git add -A
git commit -m "Baseline before reorganization"
Now any change Claude makes is undoable with git checkout . or git reset --hard HEAD. This is the foundation of the “robust system with fail-safes” principle.






Tip



Never used Git? Read Git, for economists who’ve never used it before this step. The five-minute version: Git takes snapshots of your project; every snapshot is permanent locally; you can always go back. Without Git, you have no fail-safe under what follows; with Git, every step on this page is one keystroke away from undoable.




Step 3 — Open Claude Code and take inventory
Start Claude in the copy:
claude
First prompt — purely read-only. You’re asking for a map, not an action:

“Read the entire project. Don’t modify anything. Produce a Markdown inventory with: (a) every top-level file and directory, (b) for each code file, a one-line description of what it appears to do, (c) for each data file, its size and a guess at whether it looks like raw input or derived output, (d) for each .tex file, whether it appears to be a paper draft, an old version, an appendix, slides, or something else. End with a section called ‘Open questions’ — things you’d need me to confirm before reorganizing.”

You will get back a 2-4 page document. Read it carefully. This is where you discover that analysis_v3_rebuttal.do is actually the live one and analysis.do is from two years ago — exactly the kind of thing a clean reorganization needs to get right.


Step 4 — Identify the live code path
Now narrow the inventory to what currently matters:

“Based on the inventory, identify the live code path — the minimal set of scripts and data files needed to reproduce the current version of paper.tex (or whichever .tex file I confirm is live). Trace dependencies: which scripts read which data files, which scripts produce which intermediate files, which scripts produce the tables and figures cited in the paper. Output as a Markdown list. Don’t move or delete anything yet.”

If Claude is unsure which .tex is the live paper, it will ask. Tell it.
What you get is a dependency map. Everything not on it is a candidate for archiving in step 6.






Warning



This is the step where Claude can hallucinate dependencies. Spot-check a few of its claims. Open a script Claude says produces Table 3; confirm it does. Open a .dta Claude says is unused; grep for its name across the project to make sure nothing references it. The cost of a hallucinated “this file is dead” is real — you might archive a file that something obscure actually needs.




Step 5 — Confirm and adjust the live path manually
This step is for you, not Claude. Read the dependency map. Add anything Claude missed. Remove anything you know is actually dead. The output of this step is your confirmed list of “what stays in the live path.”
A useful question to ask yourself for ambiguous files: “if this file went missing tomorrow, would I notice?” If no, archive. If yes, live.


Step 6 — Move exploration to archive/, don’t delete
Now the first real edit. Tell Claude:

“Create an archive/ directory. Move every file and folder NOT on the confirmed live-path list into archive/, preserving relative structure inside archive/ so I can find things later. Use git mv so the moves are tracked. Don’t delete anything. Show me the plan before executing.”

Use plan mode for this — Shift+Tab until you see “plan mode” before you send the prompt. You want to read the full move list before any file is touched.
When the moves are done, commit:
git add -A
git commit -m "Archive non-live files"






Tip



Why archive instead of delete? You will be wrong about what’s dead roughly 10% of the time. A coauthor will ask “what happened to the robustness check that used wage_no_outliers.dta?” and the answer “in archive/data/wage_no_outliers.dta” is much better than “I deleted it last Tuesday.”




Step 7 — Standardize the folder structure
Propose first, move second:

“I want to reorganize the live files into this structure: [paste the target structure from earlier on this page, edited for your project]. Propose how to map every current live file into the target structure. Don’t move anything yet. Flag any files where you’re not sure where they belong, and any files in the target structure that don’t exist yet (e.g., I have no master.do — that’s fine, we’ll create it later).”

Read the proposed mapping. Adjust anything that’s wrong. Then:

“Execute the mapping. Use git mv. Do not modify file contents — only move and rename. After every move, update path references in the remaining live files so the project still resolves. Cover each language’s idioms: Stata (include, do, use ... , clear, save, import delimited), R (source(), here::here(), readr::read_*(), setwd(), ggsave()), Julia (include(), using, CSV.read, joinpath(), Pkg.activate), Python (import, from ... import, pathlib.Path, pd.read_*, open()), LaTeX (\input{}, \includegraphics{}, \addbibresource{}), Matlab (addpath, cd, load, readtable). Show me each path-fix diff before applying.”

Plan mode again. Approve diffs one at a time. Commit when done:
git commit -am "Reorganize live files into standard structure"


Step 8 — Find and fix hardcoded paths

“Search the entire project (excluding archive/) for hardcoded absolute paths — anything starting with /Users/, /home/, C:\\, ~/Dropbox, or that references a specific user’s folder. List every occurrence with file and line number. Don’t change anything yet.”

You’ll get a list. For each hardcoded path, decide:

Convert to relative. Best default. /Users/me/Dropbox/wage-paper/data/raw.dta becomes data/raw/raw.dta.
Move to a config block. If the path points outside the project (a shared dataset on a research drive, say), put it in a small config.do (or config.R, etc.) at the project root and include it from each script. One place to change paths when machines change.
Document but leave alone. If the path is to a restricted-access data folder that genuinely lives elsewhere, document the requirement in the README and leave the path. Hardcoding is a feature here.

Then ask Claude to apply the conversion you decided:

“Convert paths in [list of files] from absolute to relative, assuming the project root is the working directory. Show diffs.”

Commit when done.


Step 9 — Draft CLAUDE.md
CLAUDE.md is read by Claude at the start of every session in this project. See Memory, CLAUDE.md, skills for the full picture; for now:

“Write a CLAUDE.md at the project root with: (1) one-paragraph description of what the project is and its current status, (2) the full stack — for every language used in code/, the version (Stata 18, R 4.4, Julia 1.11, Python 3.12, …) and the key packages, plus the LaTeX distribution and any Stata/R packages that aren’t on the default path, (3) folder conventions in this project (data/raw/ is read-only; output/ is built; etc.), (4) the orchestrator (make-all.sh or Makefile) and how to run it, including the order in which the languages are invoked and any language-specific gotchas (e.g., ‘the Stata binary on this machine is stata-mp’), (5) what to never do (don’t modify data/raw/, don’t commit data/derived/, don’t change paper/paper.tex without asking, etc.), (6) anything else a new collaborator would need. Read what’s already in the project to fill in real values; ask me where you’re unsure.”

Read what Claude produces. Edit it freely — this is your document. Commit.


Step 10 — Draft README.md
README.md is the human-facing version of CLAUDE.md, plus more context. Same principle: have Claude draft, you edit.

“Write a README.md at the project root following the AEA data and code availability standards: (1) project description and citation, (2) data availability and provenance — for each dataset in data/raw/, where it came from, whether it’s public or restricted, how to obtain it if restricted, (3) computational requirements — software, packages, expected runtime, (4) instructions to reproduce — exactly what command(s) someone runs from a clean clone, (5) a mapping from each table and figure in paper/paper.tex to the script and output file that produces it, (6) license. Use what’s already in CLAUDE.md and the code; ask me where you’re unsure.”







Warning



Read this draft critically. Claude can write a plausible-looking README that overstates how complete the project is. The data-availability section in particular: if your raw data came from a confidential source, say so explicitly and don’t let Claude paper over it.


Edit, commit.


Step 11 — Build a master script (the orchestrator)
If your project mixes languages — Stata cleaning, then Julia estimation, then R figures, then a LaTeX compile — no single language’s script can sit at the top. You want a language-agnostic orchestrator at the project root that calls each runner in order. A small shell script is the simplest answer; a Makefile is the upgrade path.
The prompt:

“Write a make-all.sh shell script at the project root that runs the full pipeline in order: invoke each language’s runner for the scripts in code/ (Stata for .do, Julia for .jl, R for .R, Python for .py if any), then compile paper/paper.tex. Use set -euo pipefail so the script halts on the first error. cd to the project root at the top so it works from anywhere. Print a one-line progress message before each step and a one-line success message at the end. Use relative paths.”

You’ll get something like:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")"   # always run from project root

echo "[1/4] Cleaning data (Stata)..."
stata-mp -b do code/01-clean.do

echo "[2/4] Estimating model (Julia)..."
julia --project code/02-estimate.jl

echo "[3/4] Producing figures and tables (R)..."
Rscript code/04-figures.R

echo "[4/4] Compiling paper..."
( cd paper && latexmk -pdf paper.tex )

echo "Done. Outputs in output/, paper in paper/paper.pdf."
Make it executable once: chmod +x make-all.sh. From then on, one command rebuilds the whole project: ./make-all.sh.






Note



Single-language project? If everything is Stata, a master.do at the root that dos each script is fine. If everything is R, master.R calling source() on each script works. The orchestrator matters most when you cross language boundaries; below that, use what your language gives you.








Tip



A Makefile is the upgrade. Once your pipeline is stable and slow, a Makefile pays for itself: it re-runs only what’s downstream of the file you changed. For most econ projects you don’t need it on day one — but if a single rebuild starts taking 20+ minutes, that’s the signal to convert your make-all.sh into a Makefile with proper target: prerequisite rules.








Warning



Stata’s batch flag varies by platform and version. On Mac/Linux the typical invocation is stata-mp -b do script.do; on Windows it’s StataMP.exe /e do script.do. If your group uses Stata-SE or Stata-IC, the binary names differ (stata-se, stata). Tell Claude which binary you have in CLAUDE.md so it gets it right the first time.




Step 12 — Add .gitignore

“Write a .gitignore for this project. Exclude: (a) LaTeX build artifacts: *.aux, *.log, *.out, *.toc, *.blg, *.bbl, *.synctex.gz, *.fls, *.fdb_latexmk; (b) Stata: *.smcl log files (large; usually you only want the .log ASCII version); also Stata’s per-user temp files; (c) R: .Rhistory, .Rproj.user/, .Rdata, .RData; (d) Julia: *.cov. Decide whether to commit Manifest.toml: commit it if you want bit-exact reproducibility (recommended for replication packages); leave it ignored if you want package-version flexibility while you’re still developing; (e) Python: __pycache__/, *.pyc, .ipynb_checkpoints/, .venv/; (f) Matlab: *.asv (autosaves), *.mexmaci64, *.mexmaca64, *.mexa64, *.mexw64 (compiled MEX files); (g) OS junk: .DS_Store (macOS), Thumbs.db (Windows); (h) Derived data: data/derived/**; (i) Editor cruft: .vscode/ (unless you want to commit shared settings), .idea/. Show me the file before creating it.”

After it’s in place, clean up anything that’s already tracked but should be ignored:
git rm -r --cached data/derived
git commit -m "Stop tracking derived data"






Tip



One subtle Julia decision. Project.toml should always be committed — it lists which packages your code uses. Manifest.toml is the exact-version lockfile. For an active research project, ignoring Manifest.toml is fine (and keeps merge conflicts down with coauthors). For a replication package, commit it — readers should get the exact package versions you used.




Step 13 — Run end-to-end and verify
The whole point of the orchestrator and the clean structure is that you can do this:
# In the terminal, from the project root:
./make-all.sh        # or `make all` if you went the Makefile route
Or have Claude do it:

“Run ./make-all.sh from a fresh state. If any step errors, stop and tell me what happened — don’t try to auto-fix. After it succeeds, list every file produced under output/ and paper/, confirm the paper PDF compiled without unresolved references or missing-citation warnings, and report the total wall-clock runtime.”

If the master script doesn’t reproduce something that’s in your paper, that’s a real finding — either the live code path is wrong (re-do step 4) or there’s an undocumented manual step somewhere (document it in the README).
When everything runs end-to-end, commit:
git commit -am "Reorganization complete; master script reproduces all results"


Step 14 — Compare against the original
You worked in a copy. Before throwing away the original, do one final diff:

“List every table and figure file in the original project at ~/Dropbox/wage-paper/ (read-only — don’t modify anything there). For each, find the corresponding file in this reorganized project and compare. Flag any tables or figures that exist in the original but not here (might be missing live code), or that exist here but have different content (might be a numerical regression).”

Investigate any flags. When the diff is clean, the reorganized version is your new live project. Move it back to its permanent home (out of ~/Desktop/), update any external references, and you are done.

title: Reorganizing a messy project before letting Claude Code work on it
text:
Things to be careful about






Warning



Don’t reorganize on top of the original. Always work in a copy. This is so important it’s worth repeating in a callout.








Warning



Don’t delete anything. Archive everything that’s not live. The cost of an over-aggressive archive is “I had to fish a file out of archive/”; the cost of an over-aggressive delete is rebuilding work from memory.








Warning



Watch for files that look unused but aren’t. A .dta file with no matching use command in any .do file might still be loaded by name inside an included script, or referenced from a Matlab routine, or read by a coauthor’s pre-existing pipeline. Spot-check before archiving.








Warning



If you have coauthors, talk to them before reorganizing a shared project. They have a mental model of where things are. A unilateral reorganization makes you the only person who can find anything for the next month. Better: do the reorganization on a branch, send them the new structure, get buy-in, then merge.








Warning



Be thoughtful about file timestamps. git mv preserves history but the filesystem mtime resets. If you depend on file timestamps for anything (a build system, a “newest version wins” check), document it or you’ll be confused later.








Warning



Confidential data deserves its own decision. If data/raw/ contains restricted-access data, ask yourself: was Claude reading those files during the inventory step? Are you OK with that? If not, you should have moved/symlinked the data folder before starting Claude. See Confidential data for the decision tree.

title: Reorganizing a messy project before letting Claude Code work on it
text:
When not to reorganize

Right before a deadline. Don’t reorganize the night before a submission. The risk of breaking something silently outweighs the benefit.
For a project you’re about to abandon. If this paper is dead and you’re not coming back, the reorganization is wasted effort. Just archive the whole folder.
Without a copy. Yes, third time. Don’t.
For someone else’s published replication package without their permission. That has its own workflow — see the replication-package audit example.

title: Reorganizing a messy project before letting Claude Code work on it
text:
A realistic time budget
For a typical mid-sized econ project (one paper, 20-40 code/data/text files in a few hundred MB), expect:

Steps 1-2 (copy + git init): 5 minutes
Steps 3-5 (inventory + live-path identification): 30-60 minutes, most of it you reading what Claude produced and confirming
Steps 6-7 (archive + reorganize): 30 minutes
Step 8 (paths): 15-30 minutes
Steps 9-12 (CLAUDE.md, README, master script, .gitignore): 60-90 minutes, again mostly your editing and judgment time
Steps 13-14 (verification): 30-60 minutes if it works on the first try; longer if you discover broken dependencies along the way

So: half a day to a full day of focused work. The first time you do this it will take longer because the steps are unfamiliar. The second time it goes much faster. By the third project, you’ll have a personal checklist and it will feel routine.

title: Python — pandas, statsmodels, and notebooks
text:
Outline

Setup. Point Claude at a Python project. If you use uv, poetry, or a plain requirements.txt, ask it to surface that.
Cleaning with pandas. “Read raw/wages.parquet with pandas. Document columns, flag suspicious values, and propose a cleaning pipeline. Show me before applying.”
Regressions. Use statsmodels.formula.api.ols or linearmodels.PanelOLS for panel data. Have Claude build a .summary() printout and a LaTeX export.
Plots. matplotlib for journal style, seaborn for quick EDA.
Notebook vs. script. Claude works equally well in .ipynb and .py. For replication packages, prefer .py — easier to diff, easier to run from the command line.

title: Worked example — editing a LaTeX paper
text: This walks through using Claude Code on a paper draft. The tasks are intentionally pedestrian — they’re the kind of thing you’d otherwise hand to an RA, except the loop here is minutes instead of days.
crumbs: Worked example — editing a LaTeX paper

title: Worked example — editing a LaTeX paper
text:
Setup
cd ~/Desktop/papers/wage-paper
claude
Before doing anything, give Claude an orientation pass:

“Read the project. Tell me what’s here, what paper.tex is about in one paragraph, and which auxiliary files (.bib, tables, figures) it depends on.”

This takes 30 seconds. The benefit is that subsequent prompts can refer to “the main paper” or “the auxiliary files” without you re-explaining each time.
crumbs: Worked example — editing a LaTeX paper

title: Worked example — editing a LaTeX paper
text:
Task 1 — bibliography cleanup
Bibtex files rot. Entries get added during a co-author binge and never cleaned up; some are cited, some aren’t, some have subtly wrong years.

“Look at every \cite, \citet, and \citep in paper.tex and appendix.tex. List entries in references.bib that are never cited. Don’t delete anything — just give me the list.”

You’ll get something like:
Unused entries (12 of 87):
  - smith2003
  - jones1999  (note: cited as `jones99` elsewhere — possible typo)
  - ...
The flag on jones1999 is a real win: it’s the kind of thing you’d miss on a manual pass. Now:

“Remove the unused entries from references.bib. For jones1999, fix the citation key inconsistency: replace \cite{jones99} with \cite{jones1999} everywhere, and keep the jones1999 entry.”

Read the diff before approving. Compile. Done.
crumbs: Worked example — editing a LaTeX paper

title: Worked example — editing a LaTeX paper
text:
Task 2 — table reformatting
You inherit a paper from a co-author and the tables are a mix of hand-written tabular environments, booktabs, and one orphaned longtable. You want everything on booktabs with a consistent style.

“Show me the source of each table environment in paper.tex and the standalone .tex files in tables/. Identify which use \toprule, \midrule, \bottomrule (booktabs) and which still use \hline. Don’t change anything yet.”

Once you see the inventory:

“Convert all \hline-based tables to booktabs style: \toprule at the top, \midrule between header and body and around any subgroup, and \bottomrule at the end. Keep column alignments and content untouched. Make sure \usepackage{booktabs} is in paper.tex.”







Warning



Here is where you must read the diffs carefully. Table edits are the classic place where an LLM “tidies up” content you didn’t ask it to tidy — a stray digit gets reformatted, a column header gets rephrased. Read every diff and reject anything that touches the content rather than the formatting.
crumbs: Worked example — editing a LaTeX paper

title: Worked example — editing a LaTeX paper
text:
Task 3 — a careful section rewrite
This is the one where you should slow down. Claude can rewrite prose beautifully and confidently, including arguments you don’t actually make. Treat this as collaborative editing, not delegation.

“Read section 3 (Empirical Strategy) of paper.tex. Don’t change anything yet. Tell me: (a) what the central identification claim is in your reading; (b) any place where the text references something that’s not in the data section or the appendix; (c) any sentences that are longer than 35 words or have more than two subordinate clauses.”

That’s an audit, not a rewrite. Read what it says.
If you agree with the audit:

“Rewrite only the sentences you flagged in (c) for length. Preserve every claim. Do not introduce new arguments. Do not change any numbers or citations. Show me the diff sentence by sentence.”

Approve, reject, or tweak each sentence individually. You stay the author.
crumbs: Worked example — editing a LaTeX paper

title: Worked example — editing a LaTeX paper
text:
Task 4 — compile and check

“Run latexmk -pdf paper.tex and tell me if there are any errors, warnings, or unresolved citations.”

Claude runs the build, parses the log, and tells you what’s broken. If a table now has a misaligned column, you’ll find out before you re-read the PDF.
crumbs: Worked example — editing a LaTeX paper

title: Worked example — editing a LaTeX paper
text:
What this saved you

Bibliography cleanup: ~2 hours of grunt work compressed to ~10 minutes of supervision.
Table reformatting: would have taken half a day; now ~15 minutes.
Section audit: the slowest task, but most valuable — Claude is willing to flag long sentences your eye no longer sees.

title: Worked example — editing a LaTeX paper
text:
What it did not do

It did not decide what your contribution is.
It did not check whether your identification strategy is credible — it read what you wrote and described it back to you.
It did not fact-check your citations against the cited papers.

These remain your job.

title: Worked example — editing a LaTeX paper
text:
Common traps in this workflow






Warning



Don’t let it “improve” prose you didn’t ask it to. Tell it explicitly what to change and what to leave alone. “Don’t introduce new arguments” is a sentence worth typing every single time.








Warning



Don’t trust new citations it adds. If it adds a \cite{...} for a paper you didn’t tell it about, treat that as a hallucinated citation until you’ve personally confirmed the entry exists in your .bib and the cited claim matches the source. See Hallucinations.








Tip



Use plan mode for multi-file edits. Hit Shift+Tab until you see “plan mode”, then ask. Claude will write a plan (“I’ll change these 4 files, here’s what each change does”), wait for your approval, and only then edit.

title: Worked example — auditing a replication package
text:
The single highest-value use of agentic coding for an empirical economist is replication-package work. Whether you’re preparing a package for submission, refereeing one, or trying to run a coauthor’s old project on a fresh machine, the pattern is the same: someone has to read every file, trace dependencies, and figure out why the master script breaks on line 237. Claude Code is unusually good at this.
This page walks through both directions: auditing a package you’ve inherited or are refereeing, and building one from your own working project for journal submission.
crumbs: Worked example — auditing a replication package

title: Worked example — auditing a replication package
text:
Setup
cd ~/Dropbox/Projects/wage-paper-replication
claude
Same orientation pass as always:

“Read the project. List every file. For each subfolder, tell me what it appears to contain. Identify any ‘master’ script — something a user would run to reproduce the results.”

title: Worked example — auditing a replication package
section: Direction A — auditing an existing package
text:
Direction A — auditing an existing package

Step 1 — produce a dependency map

“I want a dependency map of this replication package. Trace which scripts read which raw data files, which scripts produce which intermediate data files, which intermediate files are inputs to which analysis scripts, and which analysis scripts produce which tables/figures in the paper. Output as a Markdown list. Don’t run anything yet.”

This is the kind of task that takes a careful human a full day. Claude will do it in a few minutes, and it will catch things like “table_3.do reads clean_data_v2.dta but no script in the package produces clean_data_v2.dta — only clean_data_v3.dta.” That’s the bug you’re hunting for.


Step 2 — identify what’s missing

“Based on the dependency map, list everything required to reproduce this paper that is not in the package: missing raw data files, missing intermediate files that no script produces, packages or libraries used in the code but not declared, hard-coded paths that point outside the package.”

Claude will give you a clean punch list. Common findings:

A path like /Users/coauthor/Dropbox/... hardcoded into a .do file.
A library(haven) call without haven declared in a requirements.R or renv.lock.
A merge step that requires a file you got from the IRB and didn’t put in the package.



Step 3 — try to actually run it

“Try to run the master script. If you hit an error, stop, tell me what happened, and propose a minimal fix. Don’t auto-fix anything — just propose.”

This is the test that matters. A package that “should run” and a package that runs on a clean machine are different things. Claude is patient about this loop in a way humans are not.






Warning



For Stata, R, etc., Claude can call out to your installed interpreter. Make sure you’re running in the right environment — the same Stata version your coauthor used, the same R packages, etc. If you’re refereeing, this is part of the audit: the package should declare its environment.




Step 4 — document the gaps

“Write a REVIEW.md that lists everything I’d ask the authors to fix before this package is ready for publication. Group by severity: blockers (won’t run at all), important (runs but doesn’t reproduce a result), minor (style/clarity).”

You now have your referee report’s “replication” section, drafted in 30 minutes instead of 3 days.

title: Worked example — auditing a replication package
section: Direction B — building a package from your own project
text:
Direction B — building a package from your own project
You’ve got a paper accepted; the journal wants a replication package.

Step 1 — inventory what you actually used

“Look at every script in this project. List the ones that produce something cited in paper.tex (a number, a table, a figure). Anything not on that list is dead code or exploratory work that doesn’t belong in the public package.”



Step 2 — produce a clean structure

“Propose a folder structure for a public replication package: separate raw data, intermediate data, code, output. Don’t touch the files yet — just propose the layout.”

Approve the proposal.

“Now reorganize accordingly, copying (not moving) files from the current project into a new replication-package/ directory. Update path references in scripts so the package is self-contained.”







Warning



Have Claude copy, not move. Replication-package surgery is a one-way trip if you let it move things; you want your working project untouched until you’re sure the package builds.




Step 3 — write the README the way the AEA wants it

“Write a README.md for this replication package following the AEA data and code availability standards: data sources and access, computational requirements (software, packages, expected runtime), instructions to run, and a mapping from each table/figure in the paper to the script and output file that produces it.”

This README is the single most important document in your package. Read it critically — Claude can write a plausible-looking one that overstates how complete the package is.


Step 4 — confirm reproducibility on a fresh state

“Pretend you’ve never seen this project before. Following only the README, run every step from scratch. Stop and tell me if anything is ambiguous, missing, or fails.”

This is the test you can’t easily run yourself — your machine has all your packages installed and your data sitting around. Claude can simulate the cold-start experience.

title: Refereeing — using Claude Code to support (not replace) your judgment
text:
Outline

What Claude can do for you

Read the paper end to end and produce a tight summary you can sanity-check against your own reading.
Cross-check claims against tables. “The text on p. 14 says the coefficient on educ is significant at 1%. Find the table this refers to and confirm the t-statistic.”
Audit the replication package if one is provided. Use the replication-package walkthrough verbatim.
Flag missing standard things — pre-trends not shown, robustness to alternative specifications not reported, clustering not justified, etc.
Draft routine sections of the report (“Summary of the paper”, “Replicability”) for you to revise.



What Claude must not do

Form your opinion. The whole point of you being the referee is your judgment about contribution, identification credibility, and fit. The model has none of these.
Write the verdict. “Reject”, “R&R”, “minor revision” — that is your call, not the model’s.
Speak in your voice without your edit. Anything you submit goes out under your name and your reputation. Rewrite, don’t paste.



Confidentiality
Refereed manuscripts are confidential. Before pointing Claude Code at one, read Confidential data. The short version: ask the editor / journal whether sending the manuscript text to a cloud LLM provider is permitted under their policy. Some journals have explicit guidance now; many do not.

title: How to ask
text:
Outline — the habits

Orientation pass first. Before asking for changes, ask Claude to read the project and summarize. Cheap; saves rework.
Separate audit from action. “Tell me what you’d change. Don’t change it yet.” — almost always the right first prompt for non-trivial tasks.
Be explicit about what to leave alone. “Don’t introduce new arguments. Don’t change numbers. Don’t reformat unrelated code.” Saying it costs nothing; not saying it costs a careful re-read.
Use plan mode for multi-file work. Shift+Tab until you see “plan mode”. Claude writes a plan, you approve, then it acts.
Quote files by name. “Read paper.tex and tell me…” works better than “look at my paper”. Names are unambiguous; descriptions aren’t.
One commit per logical change. Don’t let Claude do five unrelated things in one session — each one is harder to review and harder to roll back.

title: How to ask
text:
Outline — anti-patterns

“Make this better.” Without specifics, Claude will reformat, reorganize, and rephrase, often making it worse.
“Just trust me, run it.” For destructive operations (delete files, drop database tables, force-push), make Claude pause for explicit approval. It will by default; don’t override.
“Write a complete X from scratch.” For real research code, prefer iterative: skeleton → fill in one piece → verify → next piece.

title: What changes for your research workflow
text:
Outline
What changes:

Tedious code (variable renaming, table reformatting, replication-package cleanup, .bib fixes) becomes minutes instead of hours.
You stop avoiding small-but-annoying improvements (“I’ll fix that figure formatting later”) because the friction drops to near zero.
A second pair of eyes is always available: “what’s wrong with this regression specification?” gets a useful answer in seconds.
Onboarding to an unfamiliar codebase (your old paper from five years ago, a coauthor’s repo, a published replication package) is dramatically faster.

What does not change:

Your responsibility for the specification, identification, and interpretation. The model can suggest; you decide.
The need to read the diff before accepting code into your project.
The need to run the regression yourself before believing the number in your table.
Your research taste — what’s interesting, what’s worth doing, what the contribution is. The model has none of this and will happily help you do bad work very efficiently.
